subject: ela
intro: When you present or describe something, adding a drawing, photo, map, diagram, or other visual display can help your audience understand your ideas better. The key word is 'appropriate' — a visual should clarify or add meaning to your words. A good visual matches what you are talking about and helps the audience see something they might not understand from words alone. Not every description needs a visual, but sometimes a picture truly is worth a thousand words.

items.prompt: A student is telling her class about the different parts of a butterfly. Should she add a drawing? Why?

steps: Yes — a drawing would be very helpful here.
Body parts (antennae, wings, thorax, abdomen) are hard to describe in words alone.
A labeled diagram of a butterfly shows exactly where each part is.
The visual clarifies the description and helps the audience understand better.
solution.answer: Yes, a labeled drawing of a butterfly would help the audience see and understand each body part clearly.

items.prompt: A student is describing how excited she felt on the first day of school. Should she add a visual display? What type might help?

steps: A visual could help — but it must be relevant.
A drawing of herself on the first day (backpack, big smile, school in background) could help the audience picture the moment.
However, the feeling itself (excitement) cannot be shown in a diagram.
A visual is 'appropriate' here if it shows the scene or context, not the emotion directly.
solution.answer: A drawing of herself on the first day of school could help illustrate the scene. A visual helps 'when appropriate' — when it adds to the words rather than replaces them.

items.prompt:
A student is explaining how to make a paper airplane. Which visual would be most helpful?
A) A photo of an airplane in the sky
B) A step-by-step diagram showing each fold

steps: Option A shows a plane but does not help with the folding steps.
Option B shows each fold in the correct order — directly clarifies the instructions.
The purpose of the visual is to clarify ideas, not just to be pretty.
solution.answer: B) A step-by-step diagram of each fold — it directly clarifies the how-to instructions.

items.prompt: A student is doing a report on the solar system. She uses a drawing that shows all the planets in the correct order from the sun. Is this visual appropriate? Why?

steps: Yes — this visual is appropriate.
The order of the planets is hard to remember from words alone.
The drawing shows size differences and order at a glance.
The visual directly clarifies the information in her report.
solution.answer: Yes — the drawing directly supports the content by showing the planets in order, which words alone cannot convey as clearly.

items.prompt:
A student presents about her pet dog and brings a drawing of a random fire truck. Is this visual appropriate?
A) Yes — any picture helps a presentation.
B) No — the visual must be related to what you are describing.

steps: The presentation is about her dog, but the visual is of a fire truck — completely unrelated.
A visual should clarify or add meaning to what is being described.
An unrelated visual confuses the audience instead of helping.
solution.answer: B) No — the visual must relate to the topic being described. A drawing of her dog would be appropriate; a fire truck is not.

items.prompt:
A student is describing where her school is located. What visual would help most?
A) A drawing of her favorite toy
B) A simple map showing the school's location
items.hint: Think about what would help the audience understand where the school is.

steps: A map shows location — exactly what the student is trying to describe.
A drawing of a toy has nothing to do with location.
solution.answer: B) A simple map — it directly shows where the school is located.

items.prompt:
A student is explaining the difference between big and small dogs. What visual would help most?
A) A drawing showing a Great Dane next to a Chihuahua with a size comparison
B) A drawing of a cat
items.hint: The visual should show the difference the student is describing.

steps: Option A directly illustrates the size difference between big and small dogs.
Option B introduces a different animal — not relevant to the topic.
solution.answer: A) A drawing showing a Great Dane next to a Chihuahua — it directly illustrates the size comparison.

items.prompt:
A student is describing a fruit she has never seen before. Would a drawing help?
A) Yes — a drawing of the fruit would help the audience picture what it looks like.
B) No — drawings never help.
items.hint: Think about what a visual can show that words might struggle to describe.

steps: Describing an unfamiliar fruit in words is difficult — what color is it? What shape?
A drawing shows all these details instantly.
A visual is especially helpful when describing appearance.
solution.answer: A) Yes — a drawing of the fruit would help the audience visualize something they have never seen before.

items.prompt:
A student is presenting about her favorite song. Should she draw a picture of musical notes or a photo of her family to go with her presentation?
A) A photo of her family
B) A drawing of musical notes, a music player, or the artist who sings the song
items.hint: The visual should connect to the topic — the song.

steps: The presentation is about a song.
Musical notes, a music player, or the artist — all connect directly to the topic of the song.
A photo of her family might be mentioned in the speech but is not about the song itself.
solution.answer: B) A drawing of musical notes or the artist — these are appropriate visuals that connect to the topic of the song.

items.prompt:
When is it NOT necessary to add a visual to a description?
A) When the words already paint a very clear picture and a visual would not add new understanding
B) Never — every presentation needs a visual
items.hint: Think about when a visual adds meaning vs. when it is redundant.

steps: Visuals are added 'when appropriate' — not always.
If the description is already fully clear from words alone, a visual might not add anything.
For example, describing a simple feeling ('I was happy') does not necessarily need a drawing.
solution.answer: A) When the words already make the idea completely clear, a visual may not be needed. Visuals should only be added 'when appropriate.'
